cell example: article:p1 Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAT) is the standard treatment for osteosarcoma (OS), but patient responses vary, and conventional imaging or pathology offers limited predictive accuracy. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) are promising models for assessing drug sensitivity and tumor viability ex vivo. This study evaluated the potential of PDO-based drug sensitivity testing and organoid formation potential (OFP) to predict therapeutic outcomes in OS.
cell example: article:p2 Tumor samples from OS patients collected before and after NAT were cultured as 3D PDOs. Chemosensitivity to first-line agents was quantified via a cell inhibition weighted score (CIWS), whereas OFP was used to reflect residual tumor viability. Clinical response was assessed via RECIST 1.1 and, for the primary analysis, dichotomized as responder (CR+PR+SD) versus nonresponder (PD); survival (OS/DFS) was tracked for up to 5 years. Correlations between PDO metrics and clinical outcomes were analyzed.
cell example: article:p3 PDOs were established from 31 samples (18 pre-NAT samples and 13 post-NAT samples), including 8 paired pre/post-NAT samples. CIWS predicted NAT response assessed by RECIST 1.1 with 83.3% accuracy (pre-NAT, 15/18; 95% CI 58.6–96.4) and 5-year DFS with 84.6% accuracy (post-NAT, 11/13; 95% CI 54.6–98.1). With predefined CIWS/OFP cutoffs, Kaplan–Meier analyses showed longer DFS/OS in CIWS-sensitive and OFP-II/III (low growth) groups (P<0.05).
cell example: article:p4 PDOs demonstrated promise as an ex vivo approach to evaluate whether ex vivo chemosensitivity and residual tumor viability measured by PDOs are associated with imaging response and 5-year survival. Their correlation with clinical outcomes highlights the potential of PDO testing to complement existing evaluation methods and to inform individualized treatment strategies.
cell example: article:p5 • Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) were successfully established from 31 osteosarcoma samples (18 pre- and 13 post-neoadjuvant chemotherapies) collected from 23 patients.

unit.explanation: The comparison is made for paired cases, each representing one patient with a pre-NAT organoid and post-NAT radiologic assessment.

platform.explanation: Predictions came from patient-derived osteosarcoma organoid drug-response testing.

readout.explanation: Drug response was measured by the standard cell inhibition rate, a viability/inhibition readout, and aggregated into CIWS.

direction.explanation: CIWS >= 5+ was classified as sensitive/predicted SD, while CIWS < 5+ was resistant/predicted PD.

threshold_rule.explanation: A fixed CIWS cutoff of 5+ was used to binarize predictions.

threshold_timing.explanation: The methods explicitly define the CIWS >= 5+ rule before comparing predictions with RECIST outcomes.

patient_mapping.explanation: The parsed XML tables contain no rows, and the required 18 patient-level assay/outcome pairs are available only as an untranscribed table image in the current evidence.

regimen_match.explanation: CIWS aggregates sensitivity to the clinically administered MAPI regimen: methotrexate, doxorubicin, cisplatin, and ifosfamide.

n_units.explanation: The reported denominator is 18 paired cases with pre-NAT organoid predictions and post-NAT radiologic assessments.

split.explanation: The report describes direct concordance in the evaluated patient cohort rather than a held-out test or cross-validated model.

headline.blocked_reason: Missing independently transcribed patient-level evidence for all 18 cases: each patient ID, pre-NAT CIWS score or binarized CIWS prediction at the >=5 threshold, and paired post-NAT RECIST 1.1 outcome (CR/PR/SD versus PD). Table 3 is supplied only as an image and has not been transcribed through read_figure; aggregate 15/18 counts alone are insufficient for row-level reconstruction.

notes: The article reports 15/18 correct classifications, accuracy 83.3%, sensitivity 4/5 for PD, and specificity 11/13 for SD.
A figure/table transcription is required before records can bind assay scores and clinical truths to source cell references.
